one_liner: Rust implementation of the Mison speculative JSON field extractor; pulls named fields 2-4x faster than serde_json in its benchmark.
what_it_does: Pikkr pulls a fixed set of fields out of a stream of JSON object records without building a DOM or tokenizing the whole record. You build `Pikkr::new(&queries, train_num)` from dot-path queries such as `$._id.$oid`, then call `parse(&mut self, record)` once per record. Each call returns `Vec<Option<&[u8]>>`: raw, unvalidated byte slices borrowed from the input, so strings keep their quotes and escapes and numbers stay as text. It does not replace serde_json: it cannot deserialize into Rust types, cannot serialize, and cannot give access to the whole document.
how_it_is_fast: It implements Mison (Li et al., VLDB 2017). SIMD byte compares (AVX2 through the x86intrin crate in the published crate) build bitmaps of backslashes, quotes, colons and braces. Bit tricks then turn those into a string mask and per-depth 'leveled colon bitmaps', a structural index that lets the parser hop between the colons at one nesting level and skip everything else. For the first train_num records ('basic parsing') it records which colon position each queried field sat at. After that, 'speculative parsing' checks only those positions and falls back to basic parsing on a miss. Values come back as slices, so nothing is allocated or unescaped per value.
when_to_use: Large NDJSON or record-per-line scans (logs, event exports, analytics dumps) where you need a few fields from each record of a few KB and the records share one or a few layouts.
Projection or filter pushdown where raw JSON text is enough and you convert only the fields you keep, e.g. comparing an ID slice or passing a sub-object through verbatim.
Throughput-bound batch jobs on x86-64 CPUs with AVX2 where you can pin an old nightly toolchain or vendor and port the code.
As a small, readable Rust reference for Mison's leveled colon bitmaps and pattern-learning speculation, to port or vendor into your own code.
when_not_to_use: You need validation. Invalid JSON is accepted and stray bytes can end up in values: open issue #9 shows `{"x":0,}` returning `0,`.
You need fields inside arrays, array indexing, or wildcards. Queries support only `$.a.b` object paths, and a path through an array returns a wrong slice (open issue #72 gets `true}]`).

Records vary in layout or queried fields are often missing. Each speculation miss falls back to basic parsing, and position statistics are learned only during the training window, so layout drift after training keeps hitting the slow path.
You need a current toolchain. The published 0.16.0 depends on x86intrin, which uses nightly-only features. Issue #76 (2024) reports it does not build on Rust 1.80.0, and docs.rs failed to build it.
You need typed deserialization, serialization, or a DOM: this crate does not provide them.

integration.dependencies: fnv; x86intrin 0.4.x (always required in the published 0.16.0; optional behind the `avx-accel` feature on the unpublished git master)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust nightly for crates.io 0.16.0 (README pins rustc 1.22.0-nightly 2017-09-07). Issue #76 reports it fails on 1.80.0. The unpublished master's CI targeted stable, beta and nightly in 2017 without avx-accel, but this is not verified on current rustc.
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 for the published 0.16.0, built with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native". Git master adds a portable scalar SWAR emulation of the AVX2 ops when `avx-accel` is off; that path is not benchmarked.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. `parse` takes `&mut self`, and the parser holds a RefCell plus its learned stats, so use one instance per thread; each instance trains separately.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false — a different API: path strings go in and raw byte slices come out. There are no serde traits and no typed or Value results.

gotchas: Results are raw JSON text. Strings include their quotes and escape sequences, and objects and arrays come back verbatim, so you still have to parse and unescape what you keep.
Keys are matched as raw bytes, and queries are split on '.'. You cannot query keys that contain a dot, and an escaped key in the data will not match its unescaped query.
One call handles exactly one JSON record, so you split the stream yourself; the benchmark splits on newlines with BufReader::lines.

crates.io 0.16.0 (2017-09-10) is older than the master branch. The AVX2-free fallback (PR #65, 2017-09-12) was never published. Cargo metadata says MIT/Apache-2.0, while the repo LICENSE and GitHub say MIT.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: For Rust, simd-json and sonic-rs are maintained and beat serde_json on full parsing, and sonic-rs builds on stable Rust with a `get` by pointer path that returns a raw LazyValue and handles array indices. Pick pikkr over them only to study or port Mison-style trained speculative skipping over many uniform records. In C++, the Mison paper entry and its structural-index successors Pison and JSONSki are the better starting points.
verified_claims_summary: The first-party rust-json-parser-benchmark reads a ~1.09 GB file (companies.json repeated 14 times; 263,214 lines averaging 4,160 bytes) line by line and times extraction of 1-16 paths per record. At 1 field, pikkr 0.16.0 reached 954 'mb/sec' untrained and 1,425 after 100 training records, vs 452 for serde_json 1.0.3; at 16 fields it reached 816 and 966 vs 232. The build used rustc 1.22.0-nightly (2017-09-07) with -C target-cpu=native on a 2-core 3.3 GHz Intel Core i7 MacBook Pro. Inside the timed region, the serde_json target (a DeserializeSeed that skips unwanted keys with IgnoredAny) builds a serde_json::Value for each hit and re-serializes it with to_string(), while pikkr returns borrowed slices. The 'mb/sec' figure uses 1024*1024 divisors, so it is really MiB/s.
status_note: Abandoned since 2017-09-21: the last crates.io release was 0.16.0 on 2017-09-10, docs.rs failed to build it, and it has no crates.io reverse dependencies. It is MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but expect to port the x86intrin AVX2 path to std::arch (issue #71 already pointed to stdsimd) before it builds on a modern toolchain.
